question:
Non-African Poetry: William Butler Yeats - Selected Poems
With close reference to four (4) poems, discuss Yeats' fascination with 'beautiful lofty things'.
modelAnswer:
'Beautiful Lofty Things' is the title of one of Yeats's Last Poems (1938), in which he lists people and moments he admired: John O'Leary's noble head, his father standing up to a hostile audience at the Abbey Theatre, Standish O'Grady speaking, Lady Gregory's courage, and Maud Gonne at Howth station, 'Pallas Athene in that straight back and arrogant head'. He ends: 'All the Olympians; a thing never known again.'

This fascination with noble, heroic and beautiful things runs through his poetry:
1. 'Beautiful Lofty Things': heroic individuals of his generation are compared to Greek gods.
2. 'No Second Troy': Maud Gonne's beauty is 'like a tightened bow', 'high and solitary and most stern'; she is compared to Helen of Troy.
3. 'The Wild Swans at Coole': the swans, 'mysterious, beautiful', represent unchanging beauty and passion, contrasted with the poet's ageing.
4. 'Sailing to Byzantium': he seeks the timeless beauty of art ('monuments of unageing intellect'), wishing to become a golden bird.
5. 'Easter, 1916': ordinary people become heroes through sacrifice: 'A terrible beauty is born.'
6. 'Coole Park, 1929' and 'In Memory of Major Robert Gregory': the aristocratic culture of Lady Gregory's house and the accomplished Robert Gregory ('soldier, scholar, horseman').
7. 'An Irish Airman Foresees His Death': the airman's 'lonely impulse of delight'.

Yeats admires nobility of spirit, aristocratic grace, heroism, beauty and art, and laments that such things are passing away in a commercial age.
(Any four poems, well discussed, earn the marks.)

subject: Literature
question:
Non-African Poetry: William Butler Yeats - Selected Poems
Yeats looks backward rather than forward in his poems. With close reference to three (3) poems, justify this assertion.
modelAnswer:
The assertion is largely true: Yeats often looks back with nostalgia:
1. 'September 1913': he contrasts the greedy, money-minded Ireland of his time with the heroic patriots of the past (Edward Fitzgerald, Robert Emmet, Wolfe Tone): 'Romantic Ireland's dead and gone, / It's with O'Leary in the grave.'
2. 'The Wild Swans at Coole': he remembers counting the swans nineteen years earlier, when 'I trod with a lighter tread'; the past was full of youth and passion, the present is ageing and loss.
3. 'Coole Park, 1929' and 'Coole Park and Ballylee, 1931': he mourns the passing of Lady Gregory's house and the aristocratic culture it represented: 'We were the last romantics.'
4. 'Sailing to Byzantium': he turns away from the modern world ('That is no country for old men') to an ideal ancient city of art.
5. Early poems ('The Wanderings of Oisin', 'The Stolen Child') draw on Irish myth and legend from a heroic past.
6. 'The Fisherman' and 'Beautiful Lofty Things' idealise figures from the past.

Yet Yeats also looks forward: 'The Second Coming' predicts a new age, and 'Easter, 1916' records a moment that will change the future ('All changed, changed utterly'). His backward look is part of his cyclical view of history, in which the past guides understanding of the future.
(Any three poems, well discussed, earn the marks.)

question:
Non-African Poetry: John Donne - Selected Poems
With close reference to four (4) poems, examine the preoccupation of John Donne in his Love Poems
modelAnswer:
John Donne (1572–1631), the leading Metaphysical poet, explores love from many angles in his Songs and Sonnets:
1. Love as a whole world: in 'The Good-Morrow' the lovers 'wake' to true love, and 'make one little room an everywhere'; each is a world to the other.
2. Defiance of the outside world: in 'The Sun Rising' he scolds the 'busy old fool, unruly Sun' for disturbing the lovers; 'She is all states, and all princes I.'
3. Love as sacred: in 'The Canonization' he asks critics to 'hold your tongue, and let me love'; the lovers will be 'canonized' as saints of love.
4. Spiritual love that survives separation: in 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning' the lovers' souls are like 'gold to airy thinness beat' and like a pair of compasses, one fixed at the centre while the other moves.
5. Physical desire and wit: in 'The Flea' the speaker argues that a flea which has bitten both lovers has joined their blood, so yielding to him is no sin.
6. Union of body and soul: 'The Ecstasy' argues that love must move from souls to bodies.
7. Cynicism and inconstancy: 'Song: Go and catch a falling star' claims no woman is 'true, and fair'; 'Woman's Constancy' mocks faithfulness.
8. Death and love: 'The Relic' and 'The Funeral' imagine love surviving after death.

Style: metaphysical conceits (far-fetched comparisons), argument and logic, dramatic openings, colloquial speech, paradox and wit.
(Any four poems, well discussed, earn the marks.)

question:
Non-African Poetry: John Donne - Selected Poems
Discuss the striking qualities of John Donne's Holy Sonnets. Refer to four (4) poems in his Selected Poems.
modelAnswer:
Striking qualities of Donne's Holy Sonnets:
1. Intense personal struggle with sin and salvation: 'Thou hast made me, and shall thy work decay?' (Holy Sonnet I) shows fear of death and despair, with hope in God's grace.
2. Defiance of death: 'Death, be not proud, though some have called thee / Mighty and dreadful, for thou art not so' (Holy Sonnet X), ending with the paradox 'Death, thou shalt die.'
3. Violent, dramatic imagery and paradox: 'Batter my heart, three-personed God' (Holy Sonnet XIV) asks God to overpower him: 'Take me to you, imprison me, for I, / Except you enthral me, never shall be free, / Nor ever chaste, except you ravish me.'
4. Vision of the Last Judgement: 'At the round earth's imagined corners, blow / Your trumpets, angels' (Holy Sonnet VII) shows the resurrection of the dead, followed by a plea for repentance now.
5. Theatrical openings and direct address to God, Death and the soul.
6. The sonnet form: mainly Petrarchan (octave and sestet), with a turn (volta), sometimes ending in a couplet.
7. Metaphysical conceits: the soul as a besieged town (XIV), life as a play ('This is my play's last scene', VI).
8. Personal grief and faith: 'Since she whom I loved' (XVII), after his wife's death, turns his love toward God.
9. Paradox and argument, as in his love poetry, applied to religion.
10. Tension between doubt and faith, fear and hope.
(Any four sonnets, well discussed, earn the marks.)

question:
African Poetry: Dennis Brutus - Letters to Martha
With reference to four (4) poems, discuss Brutus' Letters to Martha as a liberal ideological response to the apartheid system.
modelAnswer:
Letters to Martha (1968) records Brutus's imprisonment on Robben Island and is a response to apartheid from a liberal, humane standpoint (belief in human dignity, equality, freedom and justice for all races):
1. Exposure of injustice: the poems record arrest, sentence and imprisonment for opposing apartheid; Letter 1 ('After the sentence') shows the prisoner's mixed feelings on being sentenced.
2. Defence of human dignity: in Letter 2 the prisoner learns 'not to beg for favours', keeping his self-respect.
3. Description of prison conditions: 'On the Island' shows cement-grey walls and days, hard labour and monotony, revealing the system's cruelty.
4. Humane, non-violent tone: Brutus describes suffering without hatred or calls for revenge, appealing to the reader's conscience.
5. Honesty about human weakness: the letters admit fear, loneliness and the sexual frustrations of prison, showing prisoners as human beings.
6. Love of country and hope for freedom: despite suffering, he looks forward to a free, just South Africa for all.
7. The letter form itself as resistance: banned from publishing, he wrote poems as letters to his sister-in-law Martha.

So the collection is a liberal ideological response: it opposes apartheid in the name of universal human rights and dignity, using reason, endurance and moral protest rather than violent rhetoric.
(Any four poems, well discussed, earn the marks.)

subject: Literature
question:
African Poetry: Dennis Brutus - Letters to Martha
Comment on the title of the collection 'Letters to Martha'.
modelAnswer:
1. The title refers to Martha, Brutus's sister-in-law (his brother's wife), to whom the poems are addressed.
2. It reflects the circumstances of writing: as a 'banned' person he was not allowed to write or publish poetry, so he wrote his poems as letters, which could pass as personal correspondence.
3. 'Letters' suggests intimacy, honesty and personal communication: the poems speak directly about prison experience, fear, loneliness and endurance.
4. It gives the collection a confessional, testimonial quality: the letters are a record of life on Robben Island for the outside world.
5. Writing to a family member shows the importance of family ties and human contact for a prisoner.
6. The title is simple and modest, matching the restrained, conversational style of the poems.
7. Ironically, private 'letters' become public protest against apartheid.
